newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cocoa--Chadler deny rumours of factory closure.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa--Chadler deny rumours of factory closure.

text.p: Cocoa grinders Chadler have denied rumours that they are planning to close down their processing plant in Salvador and leave the dwindling Bahia cocoa trade.
"Chadler has never thought about leaving the market," a company official said.
"We will not close unless there is no more cocoa left in Bahia. We are just doing the same as the others and scaling down our operation to adjust to the times."
"It's just our enemies who are saying we will. It's unethical competition," the official added.
Chadler has been forced to reduce output because of the dramatic fall in production of Bahia cocoa in the last five years.

"We are not talking about seven million (60-kilo) bag crops any more. This year it looks like Bahia will produce 2.7 million bags. Cocoa will not disappear but I can imagine crops of 2.0 million bags over the next three or four years," he said.
"As a result we have had to restructure and we are now viable for the new reality."
The official said Chadler had reduced its workforce from 500 to 260 employees in the last two years and output from the traditional 750,000 60-kilo bags of beans processed annually to around 500,000.
"We still process around 17 to 18 percent of all the cocoa grown in Bahia," he said.

One advantage for the industries was that whereas they previously paid a premium over the export price, they now paid under the going rate. "The competition used to be very intense but today there are only four factories left and only a very small amount is exported," he said.
Chadler, who began operations in 1944, moved out of their old factory in 1994 because the neighbourhood had become mainly residential.
The company leased a factory in a different area and have two-and-half years left still to go on the contract. "At the end we intend to extend the lease or buy the factory," said the official.

On the crop front, farmers said heavy rain fell Thursday in the drought-stricken growing region which has suffered from almost two months of nearly completely dry weather. However, once again more fell in the coastal region than the interior.
Cocoa producer Ronaldo Monteiro said that the rain was too late to save the October-April midcrop, which is expected to yield 1.0 million 60-kilo bags.

Arrivals for the week ending September 8 dropped to only 25,729 bags, a clear indication that the current midcrop is quickly coming to an end. Farmers said it is likely to be several weeks before harvesting of the main crop gets into full swing.
Internal prices were between 15.0 and 15.5 Real per 15-kilo arroba but farmers complained that 17.0 Real was needed to keep up with the export price.
